image_description:
## 1. Chart type
- **Nested donut chart / sunburst chart** (multi-level radial partition chart)

## 2. Layout techniques
- Uses **hierarchical nesting** with **concentric rings**:
  - **Inner ring**: major food groups
  - **Outer ring**: subcategories within each food group
- Segments are **partitioned by angle/arc length** to represent values.
- Uses **color** to group outer-ring segments with their corresponding inner-ring category.
- No faceting or small multiples.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Food group (e.g., Protein, Dairy, Grains, Fruit, Vegetables, Other) | Categorical/nominal | Inner-ring segment identity; color/hue; text label |
| Food subcategory (e.g., Meat, Poultry, Whole fruit, Dark green vegetables, etc.) | Categorical/nominal | Outer-ring segment identity; text label |
| Weekly cost in dollars for each group/subcategory | Quantitative | Arc length/angle of segments; dollar-value labels |
| Hierarchical relationship (group → subcategory) | Ordinal/structured hierarchical categorical | Concentric ring level and containment within parent segment |
| Total weekly food plan cost ($193) | Quantitative | Center label/text |

comments.raw_comment:
I notice that in this graph it is showing us a weekly food plan for a family of 4. I also notice that the lowest being bought and eaten in this food plan is the section called "other". Which includes soda, candy, coffee, etc. I also notice that it is expected for the families to use the most money on things that are healthy for them, such as protein and vegetables. This is probably because protein and vegetables give health benefits, when the "other" section gives much of the opposite.

I wonder why the money set aside for dairy is less than most of the other sections. I would think that people would have to spend a lot of money on items like milk, and other things that give your body dairy. I suppose this is because your body needs less dairy than protein and vegetables, or maybe dairy products just cost less. 

This relates to me and my community because it could help people buy what they actually need for their bodies at the grocery store. A lot of people end up buying just a bunch of protein, and barely any other type of food like grains and vegetables, therefore not giving their body what they need. It could also show people how they can make their body healthier, by spending a lot less money on things that they need a lot less, like soda, candy, coffee and tea.

comments.raw_comment: I notice that this graph shows a healthy food plan for a family of four for a low price. I notice that there are 6 categories and 22 subcategories. The categories are color-coded and include the items that are found on a portion control plate. Protein, dairy, fruit, veggies, and grains. I notice they also include an "other" section which is for prepared foods, coffee or tea, and table fats, condiments, soda, and candy. I also notice that the graph adds up the subcategories in each large category to find the total price. then each category is added up to the total cost for a family of four to eat for a week. I wonder if this family is buying the generic versions of the food or not organic food because I feel like this would not be enough money for a family of four unless they ration it out or use very little per day. Maybe this family is not buying organic food because organic food is expensive and would definitely up the cost of a budget if you were to make one based on this. Possible title: Budgeting for a Family of Four

comments.raw_comment:
"How does your diet compare to this families diet?"

I notice that protein is the most expensive section but that whole fruit (located in the fruit section) is the most expensive item. The fruit section is actually the second cheapest even though it contains the most expensive item. The vegetables section and the protein section are tied for most amount of items. Both have five items and they are only $1 apart in cost. Dairy has three items while grains has four items. Grains is $3 more than dairy. I wonder if the closer the amount of items are the closer the price is. 
I also notice that the healthier the food the more it costs. For example candy only costs $8 while fruit is $19. 
Another thing I see is that this families diet is different from mine. I rarely get candy or anything else junk foodie like cereal, and I'm a vegetarian. I wonder if that lowers my families weekly food cost (I live in a family of four unless you count my 8 chickens and 2 cats).

Title: Food for A Family of Four

What I notice is that this graph shows a family of four's weekly food plan, showing the different products purchased. They spend the most on protein ($47), followed by vegetables ($46), then grains ($31), dairy ($28), fruit ($27), and lastly other ($14). The graph shows the different categories of foods as well as subcategories such as dark green vegetables, or seafood. Thinking about how a "normal" diet is they seem to be buying balanced meals, and the amount of processed food is limited. I also notice that the bill seems very low compared to what I have seen especially for a family of four. I wonder how old the children in the families are and if they eat more at home or eat out too. Another thing I wonder is if they were purchasing name grocery store brand products (such as Market Basket or Shaw's) or if they are buying organic which likely would greatly increase the spending amount. The last thing I wonder is that if they were to purchase more processed foods if the weekly budget would increase or decrease.

comments.raw_comment: The first thing I noticed was the infographic pie-esque chart, which makes sense as it’s the first thing presented other than the title and a miniature description. The chart has a decent breakdown consisting of a few main food groups. The chart then goes into further detail on each food group with specific foods, such as cereal, rice, and pasta within the grains category. I wonder not only what brands were bought at these prices but at what stores the items were bought. I also wonder if the fruits and vegetables are organic or not and from what state(s) most of the data is from. For my family and I’s typical spending habits, the fruits are a little inflated on the chart (we usually spend $15-$20 on fruits weekly) and the vegetables are inflated on the chart ($20-$30 weekly). The grains and dairy sections were pretty accurate. For protein, we usually spend more than the chart, spending about $60 weekly between kosher chicken, nuts, seeds, and protein bars compared to the $47 on the chart. I am also curious about the consumption of the food bought. There is a lot of food that goes to waste each week and I am curious as to how much (if any) went to waste. With many hectic schedules in corporate America, plenty Americans do not cook most of their meals and thus many of the foods could be going to waste. I also wonder how much food allergies play into how much people spent in the various categories. I would title this chart: "Mighty Meals for Four: Meals and Deals on a Budget"

comments.raw_comment:
This graph from the Department of Agriculture sets out a suggested distribution of a staple budget. They attempt to include a 'balanced' food model for an average family of 4 people for a total of $193 per week. At first sight, it seems like a massive help for many families who benefit from this resource.

On the other hand, They suggest a diet based on animal protein, which is the highest budget, $47, regardless of how harmful the number of antibiotics, hormones, and steroids added can be for daily consumption.

Nevertheless, many scientific studies have shown that the daily consumption of animal meats is directly related to cancerous diseases. Still, unfortunately, some government institutions & health organizations continue to refer people to these types of diets.

After analyzing the "Thrifty Food Plan," there is a question: is the government interested in the people's health, or is it simply looking to benefit private companies and fulfill just one more item on its agenda?

I am convinced that the government should have an essential role in educating citizens. Therefore, it is not enough to give them the money. They have to provide them the tools to make informed decisions that impact their well-being and their families. Otherwise, it would be hard to decrease the number of heart disease deaths, overweight, and diabetes.

model dietary plan illustrating how families could practically meet nutritional guidelines at a low cost:

The first thing that sticks out to me is an overall cost of $193 per week per family of 4. If my math is correct, that allocates just about $48 per family member. From my personal experiences, I feel as though $48 a week for food is quite a small number. I wonder how this typical family would feel? Are they hungry everyday? Is this budget perfect for their dietary needs? For me personally, I have Celiac disease which requires me to eat gluten free foods, which are quite expensive. Flour can be as much as $18 per bag. I wonder if this budget is able to accommodate allergies. Additionally, another big thing that sticks out to me is the importance of veggies, totaling $46 per week. The most expensive portion is protein, which I can say I expected. In its subcategory, it shows just how expensive things like chicken are. Lastly, I would title this graph: "Eating on a Budget: is cheap always good?"

This graph shows a model weekly food plan for a family of four. I noticed that the chart suggests that families of four should plan to spend more money on protein and vegetables. I also noticed that each section of the graph has a different color and that the outer sections of the circle are subsections to the inner sections.  For example cheese is a subsection of dairy.  I also noticed that the plan encourages people to be spend money on healthy foods.
I wonder if this plan can be adjusted to help families of four who have a low income.  I wonder if age affects the amount of money that a family spends. Does the SNAP plan account for people who have food allergies? Do food allergies affect the amount of money?  I also wonder if working hours affect the food plan.  If people are constantly working they have no time to cook.   I also wonder how a person can help the SNAP Program.  Can you donate food and other things to the SNAP Program to help families in need?
This relates to me because my family has four people.  Each week my family and I go grocery shopping for the school week.  I am pretty fortunate to have enough to eat in my life.  This relates to my community because there are some people in my community who can not afford to eat.  The SNAP program can help people in my community have a nice and affordable meal.
Catchy Title: Healthy and Affordable Budget

comments.raw_comment:
1. I noticed when looking in this graph that there was a wheel of food groups with suggested options and prices for specific items related to these groups. For example, Seafood was listed under Protein. The wheel adds up the total cost of what all of these foods would be for a 4 person family and comes to the conclusion that families would only have to spend near $193 per week for food. I also noticed that the healthier foods were more expensive. I know that this is generally the case everywhere because natural ingredients are not produced as quickly as artificial foods or foods that do not require growing. 
2. I wonder what the quality of all of the foods would be with such low prices. I wonder how healthy they would be if they are so cheap and it leaves me to wonder if it would be better off to spend more money on a smaller amount of natural healthy foods rather than less money on a bigger amount of preserved healthy foods. I understand that there are sacrifices that have to be made, but I believe there are smarter ways to go about these sacrifices. I also wonder if this will be enough food or if everyone will have small portions and receive the bare minimum. If this is true, I believe that this graph is deceiving because it makes it seem like you get more for less. 
3. I relate to this because I know how expensive foods can be and I know that people's health can be put at risk in order to survive. 
4. Headline: "Is It Worth It or a Waste?: Spend Less Get More SNAP Plan

comments.raw_comment:
The first thing I noticed was the color coordination. When I was younger and in elementary school, they used to called a balanced diet a "rainbow." Meaning that you should have different types/colors of food on your plate at every meal. One thing that sticks out to me is how expensive everything is on this wheel. If you're someone working a low income or minimum wage job and are providing for your family, this seems like an impossible task. I also wonder how families who may have certain food allergies might adapt to this as well. I'm also wondering the quality of food that is listed at these prices, especially with the meat! I would imagine that it would be one of if not the highest expense. 

In my community, lack of food was never a problem which I'm incredibly thankful for. But I do know that there are several food banks in my area for those who don't have the privilege of going home with food on the table. Many have to make sacrifices, whether it is a balanced diet or cutting down on other necessities in order to properly nourish themselves. 

Headline: The real cost behind your grocery trips

1. I notice that the costs are relatively spread out across different varieties of food. The cumulative cost is quite a bit, but it isn't dominated by any one kind of food.

2. I wonder what the relative amounts typically bought in each category of food are. If you buy enough of any food, its going to cost alot, but it would be interesting to see which categories of food cost more money for the same amount. I realize this could be hard to measure because different foods are measured in different ways, but it could at least give us a sense of how much of a certain food cost a given amount. I also wonder what 'Potatoes.com' means.

3. I am a vegetarian so I personally don't need to worry about the costs of meats, though the rest of my family is not. My area has very good restraunts and pretty good grocery store food, but it can be expensive. I see the effects of cheaping out on food through my school, where the food tastes like plastic, so if someone couldn't afford quality food, they could be stuck eating plastic.

In this chart, the most money spent out of all of them are meat and vegetables, because everything in these sections are mostly, individually, more expensive than the rest. I notice that the allotted food budget for a family of four is $193 for one week, which would be $6.89 for one person each day. I notice that protein and vegetables have the highest allotment of money. The other category, which includes coffee and tea, has the least money. The sub-categories that have the most money are whole fruits, whole grain products, poultry, and low fat dairy products. The sub categories that have the least money are grain cereals and snacks, coffee and tea, cheese, and eggs. I notice that “red and orange” vegetables and “dark green” vegetables are separate categories.

I wonder why dairy is included in the graph even though it is not necessary for a nutritionally complete diet. I wonder why the vegetables are separated into different categories by color. I wonder why coffee and tea only get $2 when they are staple parts of the American diet. I wonder why whole fruit gets the most allotted money. I wonder why the graph specifies things like whole grain versus refined grain and low fat versus high fat.

This impacts my community because if 1 in 8 Americans receive SNAP aid, then there are people in my community who receive it. Also, any person may need advice for how much money to spend on what food.

Today’s graph shows the Department of Agriculture’s newly revised Thrifty Food Plan, the food groups used to estimate the cost of an economical, nutritious diet.   This plan is the basis of the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP).   Note the allocation to food groups is the basis of calculating the SNAP benefits.  Recipients can spend their benefits as they choose.  Although the payments may seem modest for middle-income Americans, the program reduces hunger, improves nutrition and lead to better health.

From 9 am – 2 pm E.T. today, share with us your responses online to these three questions plus, a catchy headline that captures the ideas in this graph. 

By Friday morning, we’ll reveal the article that included these graphs and much more.  We look forward to reading your discoveries.

Note that you can get a link to your response to share with your teacher and classmates by clicking the response box below your response “Email me when my comment is published.”  

The next “What’s Going On In This Graph?” will be released by Friday, Oct. 15 with moderation on Wednesday, Oct. 20.  The topic:  Pandemic Inflation.  Keep noticing and wondering.

comments.raw_comment: The first thing I notice is that the total a family of four on a low budget spends on groceries is $193.00 per week. I also notice that protein and vegetables cost the most per week with only a one-dollar difference between the two. The three categories, diaries, grains, and fruits are all within four dollars of each other. The category labelled as "other" is the cheapest category, which ideally should be the category that is the most nutritious and beneficial, but is not. Another thing I noticed is that the most expensive food on the chart is fruits, and the fruits cost 19 dollars. I wonder that because vegetables and poultry require more labour force and care is the reason why they are so much more expensive than everything else on the chart. I would name this graph, "The Weekly Low-Budget Family Grocery Plan"

comments.raw_comment: One thing that caught my eye in this graph is that protein and vegetables take up almost the same amount of money as each other, protein being only a dollar higher than vegetables. Cutting either of these expenses down could potentially save you a lot of money week to week. Although with that said, I also wonder where the food was bought from, because depending on location, brand, freshness, etc. the price of the food can vary and there may be less expensive options available. This graph is a useful way to break down diet plans in a simple and clear graph that may be useful to several people who find themselves struggling with their meal planning, myself included. Given the content of the graph, a headline that sounds something like "Affordable Meal Planning Cheatsheet" could work.

comments.raw_comment: When looking at this graph, "Thrifty Food Plan," many things stick out to me. I notice that the biggest amount of spending goes towards protein and vegetables, paying $47 for protein and $46 for vegetables. This seems very reasonable because those two food categories should be focused on the most when it comes to shopping. The other biggest spending categories are dairy, grains, and fruit. These are also very reasonable spending amounts because each one is a staple to a healthy diet. I wonder why they only leave $2 for tea and coffee when it would be very hard to buy those items for that price. I also wonder how achievable spending $193 a week for a family of four is. In my community, groceries are not inexpensive at all, especially depending on the store you shop at. If you shop at King's then the cost of the products will differ from products at Shoprite. I still do believe this is a great way of showing families that money can be saved when it comes to buying healthy food at the grocery store, but I am not too sure how achievable it truly is. I also notice that if these budgets are placed on food weekly then how quickly would they run out. This graph shows a food budget of $193 weekly for a family of four. I wonder why this is a weekly budget when, in a sense, it seems hard to consume a lot of these foods in a week as a family. In conclusion, this is a great outline to help families budget. A catchy headline is "Weekly Grocery Store Run for a Family of Four."

comments.raw_comment:
What do you notice? 
This graph shows the weekly cost an average family of four spends on food. This average comes to $193, with $47 being spent on protein and $46 spent on vegetables. The price of these two contribute too close to half of the total cost. 

What do I wonder?
As I previously mentioned, protein and vegetables contribute to about half the amount of cost spent by families on food weekly. I wonder is this due to families having more of a need for protein and vegetables or is it more closely related to the cost of the products?

How does this relate to you or your community?
My parents go out weekly and buy the groceries for the week and likely have a budget similar to the one in this graph. Seeing each meal is close to $7 it makes me feel more grateful with what my parents are able to give me.

"Food for Thought"
